title: Survivable networks, linear programming relaxations and the parsimonious property
contribution: Proves that, under the triangle inequality, degree-tightness (parsimonious) constraints do not change the LP relaxation value of the survivable-network cut formulation, and derives from it exact relations between the Steiner, k-connected and Held–Karp bounds plus tight worst-case ratios of two tree heuristics against the LP bound.
problem_entry: {IO; LO as engine} The SNDP (Steiner tree, k-connected design and, with degree constraints, the TSP as special cases) is NP-hard, which typically sends researchers to approximation and local search (p. 2), and its LP relaxation is polynomial but has no practical algorithm (p. 4); the paper enters through a structural property of that relaxation (p. 3).
key_idea: Parsimonious property (Theorem 1, p. 5): forcing minimum degrees at any vertex set leaves the LP value unchanged under the triangle inequality; consequences: Steiner vertices removable, Steiner LP = HK/2, k-connected LP = (k/2)·HK, HK bounds the 2-connected problem and is monotone (pp. 3, 8–9); tree and improved tree heuristics analysed against the LP bound (pp. 10–18).
assumptions: Complete graph, repeatable edges, r_ij = min(r_i, r_j) for the heuristics (pp. 4, 10); triangle inequality made harmless by shortest-path closure (Theorem 3, pp. 6–7); rational data (p. 6); divisibility of connectivity types for tightness (p. 13); no data sets.
proof_devices: scale a rational LP optimum to an even-integral Eulerian multigraph and split off edge pairs with a strengthened Lovász lemma (Lemma 2, pp. 5–6; Appendix 1, pp. 19–20)
metric closure without loss of generality by path rerouting (Theorem 3, pp. 6–7)
heuristic value written as an LP over Edmonds' spanning-tree polytope; the scaled LP optimum is feasible there, giving 2 − 2/|S| (Theorem 7, p. 11)
symmetric tightness: an integrality-gap instance and a heuristic-gap instance (pp. 11–12, Figs. 2–3)
telescoping over connectivity levels plus monotonicity (Theorem 8, pp. 12–13); recursive tight construction (Theorem 9, p. 13; Appendix 2, pp. 20–21); Θ(log r_max) and Θ(p) (Corollary 10, p. 14)
decompose the optimal IP network into a 2-connected block plus trees, each feasible for a relaxation (Theorem 11, pp. 14–15)
Edmonds' perfect-matching polytope for the improved tree heuristic (Theorem 13, p. 17)
partition bounds for Euclidean instances from subadditivity and upperlinearity (pp. 9–10)
experiments: none of its own (n/a); relies on Johnson's reported Held–Karp study, heuristic tours within 1% of optimal for up to 100,000 vertices (p. 7), and on HK above 99% of the optimal tour (p. 8).
positioning: Extends Held–Karp, Lovász splitting and Edmonds' polytopes (pp. 5, 7, 9, 11, 17); strengthens the 2 − 2/|S| Steiner MST-heuristic results by measuring against the LP bound (pp. 3, 11); re-derives Cunningham's result (p. 8); credits Agrawal–Klein–Ravi, Goemans–Williamson and Bienstock et al. with extensions (pp. 18–19); subsumes rather than attacks.
writing: One named property with 'numerous consequences' (p. 1); results flagged 'surprising' or 'astonishing' (pp. 3, 5, 9); roadmap paragraph (p. 3); long proof sketched in an appendix (p. 14); figures of worst-case instances (p. 12); little hedging.
limits_future: The property fails without the triangle inequality (p. 6), absorbed by Theorem 3; no practical algorithm for the general LP (p. 4); tightness only under divisibility (p. 13); heuristics never run; future: degree constraints (k-TSP) and odd-cut (matching-type) problems (p. 18).

method_links.note: Reads structure off the relaxation of a classical IP formulation and prints the boundary with tight instances, but rewrites no other tradition's problem and uses no dual. Correction for SKILL.md's Domain Map (IO row), which cites this DOI for 'LP-relaxation rounding': the paper has no rounding step; it bounds MST and matching constructions by the LP value (pp. 10–18).

The bound-as-certificate idea of step 4 in theory form: HK bounds certified heuristic tours within 1% (p. 7), and the k-connected LP is 'a very good lower bound' to judge heuristic networks (p. 9); no computation, no duel.

Already separates polynomial solvability from practicality ('not satisfactory in practice', p. 4), an early root of the 2019 principle; but faced with NP-hardness takes the approximation route it calls typical (p. 2), the belief Method 2 later concedes was right when formed and reopens with MIO solvers.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The LP relaxation is the object of study, the yardstick for heuristics and an algorithmic lever (Steiner and k-connected LP values computed by Held–Karp's method).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: bound, constructive heuristic, provable ratio, tightness instance
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Tree heuristics bounded by the LP value, with tight families in both directions.

transferable: Before using triangle-inequality arguments, replace costs by shortest-path distances and prove that the IP and LP values do not change (Theorem 3, pp. 6–7).
Scale a rational LP optimum to an even-integral Eulerian multigraph so that graph lemmas such as splitting off apply without raising cost (p. 6).
Bound a heuristic against the LP by writing its value as an LP over a known integral polytope (spanning tree, perfect matching) and showing that a scaled LP optimum is feasible there (pp. 11, 17).
Prove tightness in both directions: an integrality-gap family and a heuristic-gap family (pp. 11–12).
Sharpen a constant by splitting an optimal integral solution into parts that are each feasible for a different relaxation (Theorem 11, pp. 14–15).

quotes.text: The variety of consequences makes the parsimonious property particularly important.
Typically, such a negative result from complexity theory leads researchers to obtain approximate rather than optimal solutions.

title: Stochastic and dynamic vehicle routing with general demand and interarrival time distributions
contribution: Extends heavy-traffic analysis of the dynamic traveling repairman problem from uniform locations and Poisson arrivals to general densities and renewal arrivals, with a factor-2 stronger lower bound, TSP-batching policies within about 1.8 of it for spatially unbiased and biased service, and closed-form results on how demand non-uniformity and an equal-service constraint change the optimal system time.
problem_entry: {SD + AP; CP as a device} The authors' own DTRP results assumed uniform locations and Poisson arrivals, rare in practice (p. 3), and their proofs relied on uniformity and PASTA, forcing new techniques (p. 3); applications from couriers and repair crews to automobile distribution (p. 2).
key_idea: Spatial queues on shrinking balls make the thinned renewal input Poisson-like (Lemma 2, pp. 7–8), giving a nearest-neighbour lower bound with the waiting-demand density φ left free (Lemmas 3–5, pp. 8–11); φ = f for unbiased policies (Theorem 1, p. 11) and a convex program with a KKT closed form for biased ones (Theorem 2, pp. 11–12); batch-and-TSP policies on equal-probability or density-sized cells match the bounds within about 1.8 (Theorems 3 and 5, pp. 13, 17).
assumptions: Bounded planar region; stationary renewal arrivals with finite variance; i.i.d. general service times; i.i.d. locations with a K-Lipschitz density bounded above and below (pp. 3–4); policy class P1–P3, P3 'needed primarily for technical reasons' (pp. 4–5); heavy-traffic limit ρ → 1 (p. 4); piecewise-uniform densities smoothed in an ε-strip (pp. 16–17); simulation data only (p. 21).
proof_devices: spatial queues and Little's law define the time-average density φ (pp. 5–6)
renewal thinning into a vanishing ball plus the Bertsimas–Nakazato heavy-traffic relation, a substitute for PASTA (Lemma 2, pp. 7–8)
stability condition plus nearest-neighbour bound (Lemmas 3–5, pp. 8–11)
convex program over φ, Lagrangian dual and KKT sufficiency giving a closed form (Theorem 2, pp. 11–12)

TSP asymptotics (Beardwood–Halton–Hammersley, Steele), Karp–Steele variance and the Iglehart–Whitt heavy-traffic formula for superposed renewal inputs, then batch size optimized by a change of variables (pp. 13–16)

Hardy–Littlewood–Pólya inequality: uniform demand is worst and biased service strictly better for non-uniform densities (Proposition 1, pp. 23–24); a two-region density with an unbounded unbiased/biased ratio (pp. 24–25)
tightness audit: an 'optimal removal rule' meets Lemma 4's bound exactly (Theorem 6, pp. 25–27)
extensions: Haimovich–Rinnooy Kan tour partitioning for capacitated vehicles (Theorems 7–8, pp. 28–29); d dimensions with asymptotic optimality as d → ∞ (Theorem 11, p. 30)
experiments: Simulation of space-filling-curve and nearest-neighbour policies on a two-region piecewise-uniform density (ε = 10⁻⁴, λ = 1, s = 0.1, σ² = 0, ρ = 0.8; one run for each of 11 values of δ from 0.05 to 0.9999; code of the earlier paper) (p. 21); log–log regression slopes 0.80 and 1.37 estimate distributional exponents 0.44 and 0.58 (pp. 22–23); no replications or confidence intervals.
positioning: Continues and corrects the authors' own OR 1991 and 1993 papers: the new bound is 'weaker' in being asymptotic but general and twice as large (p. 11); imports applied and geometric probability (PASTA p. 3; Iglehart–Whitt p. 14; BHH, Steele, Karp–Steele pp. 13–14; Rhee p. 30) and routing heuristics (Bartholdi–Platzman p. 20; Haimovich–Rinnooy Kan p. 28); reuses his own distributional Little's law with Nakazato (p. 7).
writing: Abstract lists four claims (p. 1); practical reasons for generalizing before theoretical ones (p. 3); conjecture labelled with its basis, 'heuristic arguments' (p. 16); intuition after the unbounded example (p. 25); self-critical asides that the bound is likely weak and the 1.83 guarantee 'too pessimistic' (pp. 27–28); conclusion turned into planning uses (p. 31).
limits_future: Heavy traffic only; technical policy class (p. 5); asymptotic optimality of the unbiased policy only conjectured (p. 16); no tight example for the biased bound (p. 27); optimal tours difficult to compute in practice (p. 20); future: strategic models for terminal location, fleet sizing and districting (p. 31) and a proof of the conjecture (p. 16).

method_links.note: An applied-probability question (the best heavy-traffic system time over spatially biased policies) becomes a convex program over the performance density φ with a closed-form KKT solution; step 5 (print the boundary) is the Section 6 tightness audit. A routing-side precursor of the performance-space move of SW1 (achievable region), from the same years.

The price of a policy constraint: spatially unbiased service, 'perhaps imposed as a matter of policy' (p. 11), costs nothing exactly when demand is uniform and strictly more otherwise (Proposition 1, pp. 23–24), and can be unboundedly costly (pp. 24–25). No knob and no curve; a binary constraint priced by closed-form functionals, 18 years before the price-of-fairness paper (DOI 10.1287/opre.1100.0865).
Suggests estimating a policy's constants from operating data of a 'live' system to evaluate current operating practice; a suggestion only, with no owner, data or field test.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: bound, constructive policy, provable ratio, tightness check
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Heavy-traffic lower bounds with a free performance profile, batch-and-TSP policies within a constant factor, an open conjecture on the remaining gap, and asymptotic optimality as d → ∞.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: tightness audit of one's own bound
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: A non-routing removal rule meets the lower bound exactly, showing that only more routing structure can improve it.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: static methods adapted to dynamic problems
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Static routing tools (TSP tours, tour partitioning, space-filling curves) adapted into near-optimal dynamic policies, stated as a recurring finding.

transferable: Thin a renewal arrival stream into a vanishing ball so that it behaves like Poisson and PASTA-type equalities hold asymptotically (Lemma 2, pp. 7–8).
Leave the unknown performance profile free in a lower bound, then minimize the bound over all admissible profiles by a convex program solved through KKT, so one bound covers every policy (pp. 10–12).
Batch-and-tour policy design: equal-probability or density-sized cells, batches of n/k demands, FCFS service by TSP tours, batch size optimized after a change of variables (pp. 13–17).
Audit a bound by building an abstract process that meets it exactly; if one exists, a better bound must exploit more problem structure (pp. 25–27).
For policies that resist analysis, assume the analytic form found for tractable ones and estimate its exponent by log–log regression over a one-parameter family of inputs (pp. 22–23).
Meet Lipschitz-type technical assumptions for piecewise-constant inputs by ε-strip smoothing and let ε → 0 (pp. 16–17, 20).

quotes.text: In our previous analysis, uniformity and PASTA [20] were heavily exploited. We are therefore forced to develop new proof techniques that do not rely on these properties.
A recurring finding in our analysis is that static vehicle routing methods when properly adapted can yield near optimal or perhaps even optimal policies for dynamic routing problems.

title: The multi-airport ground-holding problem in air traffic control
contribution: Formulates the static deterministic multi-airport ground-holding problem as simple 0-1 integer programs whose coupling constraints carry delays along aircraft rotations, adds cancellations and an LP-rounding heuristic, and uses MPSX runs up to 6 airports and 3,000 flights to show when network effects matter.
problem_entry: {IO + AP; LO as relaxation} Congestion costs ($2 billion a year for U.S. airlines against profits rarely above $1 billion, p. 1), weather-driven capacity swings (p. 1), an FAA command center run on controllers' judgment rather than optimization (p. 1), and a single-airport literature that ignores down-the-road delay propagation (pp. 1–2).
key_idea: Time-indexed 0-1 take-off and landing assignment variables, needed because capacity constraints are not linear in delay variables (p. 3), plus one coupling constraint per consecutive flight pair of an aircraft (p. 4); without coupling the model decomposes into known single-airport problems (p. 4); three formulations P1–P3, P3 with cancellations at P2's size (pp. 4–6); an LP-rounding heuristic (pp. 6–7).
assumptions: Static, deterministic capacities (pp. 2–3); linear delay costs as an FAA and industry approximation (p. 4); airborne delay costlier than ground (pp. 1, 4); delay caps of 4–5 and 2–3 fifteen-minute periods (pp. 2–3); size driven by the number of flights (p. 5); synthetic schedules with arbitrarily chosen arrival times and capacities at the feasibility border found by trial and error (p. 8); probabilistic capacities left out (p. 12).
proof_devices: exchange argument: with infinite departure capacities, linear costs and airborne cost above ground cost, an optimum without airborne delay exists (pp. 4–5)
a posteriori computational justification of the infinite-departure-capacity assumption (pp. 5, 10)
variable elimination to assignment variables only (Appendix A, pp. 12–13)
cancellation variables with large coefficients inside the coupling constraints ('technical tricks', p. 6)
total unimodularity of the single-airport matrix (Terrab) makes the decomposed model an LP (p. 7)
LP-rounding heuristic by aircraft class: earliest period with capacity slack, cancel if none, prune the next flight's periods for coupling (pp. 6–7, 13); no guarantee proved
experiments: MPSX, no custom algorithm, CPU times only for reasonableness (p. 7); IP vs LP vs decomposed model on 1,800-flight and 1,000–3,000-flight synthetic series (2–6 airports, F'/F 0.2–0.8) plus finite departure capacities, cancellation costs, non-uniform capacities and three cost classes (Tables I–VI, pp. 8–11); network effects small with identical costs but the decomposed solution violates 180–200 of 600 couplings (p. 8), large with different costs (13,950 vs 22,811, p. 9; 22–27%, p. 10); IP times up to 25,021 CPU s (p. 9); heuristic poor at high cancellation costs, reported (p. 10); as extracted, a v_D–v_I gap of about 19% of v_I in Table II (p. 9) and a heuristic row 55% above v_L in Table IV (p. 11) are not discussed.
positioning: Claims the first multi-airport treatment (p. 2) after reviewing single-airport work by Odoni, Andreatta–Romanin-Jacur, Terrab and Richetta (p. 2); reuses Terrab's formulation and total unimodularity (pp. 5, 7); calls the FAA's identical-cost practice incorrect but well-entrenched (p. 12); no comparison with controllers' actual decisions.
writing: Abstract opens with a dollar figure and closes with a scale headline (p. 1); simplicity is the recurring selling point (pp. 2, 5, 11); rival explanations tested before the main one (p. 9); six numbered insights (pp. 11–12); candid about the heuristic's failure ('This was to be expected', p. 10).
limits_future: Static and deterministic (p. 2); size ceiling unknown (p. 12); identical costs follow FAA practice (p. 12); no deployment; future: dynamic deterministic case (Vranas 1992a, b), rolling two-hour horizons, supercomputers or special-purpose algorithms, and probabilistic capacities that 'may require a totally new approach' (p. 12).

method_links.note: The model, not the algorithm, is designed so that an existing commercial solver works (MPSX, p. 7); size depends on flights only (p. 5); the conclusion credits the formulation's simplicity for tractability (p. 11).

One joint model replaces airport-by-airport solving, whose solutions violate about a third of the coupling constraints (step 1, p. 8); IP solved to optimality with times reported, LP bound, and an LP-rounding heuristic with its failure regime printed (pp. 8–10); no warm start, no time limit, no incumbent besides the decomposed model.

Names the owner (the FAA command center) and its current rule (controllers' judgment; identical costs for all users), but the baseline is the literature's single-airport decomposition on synthetic schedules; decision metric is total delay cost; no field test.
Step 3 in practice: a thesis-lineage paper (Vranas 1992) with his own adviser Odoni as co-author, a companion Transportation Science paper, and undergraduates doing part of the computations.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The LP relaxation is near the IP value and is rounded flight by flight; its fractional share (about 10% of flights) motivated the heuristic.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: computation for structural insight, not horse races
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Runs investigate the problem's behaviour across input parameters, explicitly not the efficiency of an algorithm; CPU times only for reasonableness.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: a posteriori computational justification of a simplifying assumption
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Infinite departure capacities are assumed for the simpler model P2 and then checked against P1 runs with finite capacities.

transferable: Use time-indexed assignment variables when a capacity constraint is not linear in the natural (delay) variables (p. 3).

Model propagation through a network by one linking inequality per consecutive pair; measure its value as the gap between the coupled IP and the decomposed model and also count the decomposed solution's violated links, because a small value gap can hide infeasibility (pp. 4, 7–8).
Place test instances at the feasibility border, located by sweeping capacities, where the decision matters most (p. 8).
Test an explanation of a surprising result by perturbing the suspected cause (cost slopes of continued vs other flights) and by ruling out rival explanations with existing runs (p. 9).
Remove infeasibility by adding cancel variables with cost M, then sweep M to map the regimes in which the extension changes the answer (pp. 5–6, 10).
Drop a constraint class by an exchange argument, then check its impact computationally and report the check (pp. 4–5, 10).
coauthors: Peter B. Vranas; Amedeo R. Odoni

quotes.text: It is this simplicity, reflected in the small numbers of constraints and variables, that is responsible for the tractability of large-scale GHPs.
We solved the various instances of the problem by using the well-known commercial package MPSX, rather than any custom-tailored algorithm.

title: A technique for speeding up the solution of the Lagrangean dual
contribution: Computes LP relaxations and Lagrangean duals by running Vaidya's (or the ellipsoid) cutting-plane method in a dual space whose dimension is the number of complicating constraints, with the easy subproblem as separation oracle, giving the best worst-case operation counts for about a dozen combinatorial relaxations, with no computational test.
problem_entry: {LO + IO; CP for the nonlinear extension} Large NP-hard instances are solved through LP relaxations and Lagrangean duals (p. 1), but subgradient optimization is not known to be polynomial (p. 2); scope deliberately limited to problems already polynomial where ellipsoid-like methods give speed-ups (p. 2).
key_idea: Represent the easy polyhedron by extreme points and rays and dualize: m + 1 dual variables and a separation problem that is optimization over the polyhedron (pp. 3–4), solved by Vaidya's method in O(T(n)mL + M(m)mL) (Theorem 1, p. 4); variants for several subproblems, cost splitting, Lagrangean duals of IPs, Benders-style complicating variables and nonlinear programs (Theorems 2–6, pp. 6–10).
assumptions: Polyhedra without lines (p. 3); a linear-optimization oracle over the easy set; complexity in arithmetic operations with input size L and fast matrix multiplication (p. 4); nonlinear duals only to ε in the Turing model (pp. 10–11); stochastic programs with discrete scenarios (p. 20); no data.
proof_devices: resolution theorem plus LP strong duality: a dual with one variable per complicating constraint (p. 3)
separation equals pricing over the easy polyhedron; sliding-objective ellipsoid or Vaidya's method (p. 4)
iteration counts O(kL) for Vaidya vs O(k²L) for the ellipsoid; only Vaidya benefits from fast matrix multiplication (p. 4)

primal recovery by complementary slackness under uniqueness or by an interior-point solve over generated columns (pp. 4–5); for Lagrangean duals from a generated constraint tight at the optimum (Remark, p. 8)
cost splitting (Lagrangean decomposition) when separation is harder than optimization, e.g. polymatroids (pp. 7, 18–19)
concavity of the Lagrangean dual of an arbitrary nonlinear program (p. 10)
operation-count comparisons per application, e.g. Held–Karp O(n^3.38 L) vs O(n^6.76 L) and O(n^8 L) (pp. 12–13; Table 3, p. 21)
experiments: none: no implementation, instance or timing; worst-case operation counts only (Table 3, p. 21); practicality stated as untested and dependent on Vaidya's algorithm (p. 22).
positioning: Builds on Held–Karp, the ellipsoid method and Vaidya's algorithm (pp. 1–2); credits Chandru and Trick's independent ellipsoid approach with a different focus (p. 2; a referee pointed it out, p. 22); compares with interior-point methods and direct Vaidya (pp. 12–21); concedes where Vaidya's multicommodity algorithm wins (p. 15); uses its own S052 result as a lemma (p. 13).
writing: Strong claims up front ('the fastest way to solve them', pp. 1–2; 'Surprisingly', p. 2), hedging concentrated in the concluding section (p. 22); applications as illustrations, not exhaustive (p. 12); summary tables 'for future reference' (p. 11).
limits_future: Practicality untested (p. 22); primal solutions only under uniqueness or at extra cost for (P1)–(P3) (p. 11); nonlinear duals approximate (p. 11); future: scheduling and sequencing, stronger duals by Lagrangean decomposition, hybrids with subgradient methods for practical algorithms (p. 22).

method_links.note: Duality is the central device (step 4, 'Dualize'), but used to shrink the dimension of a computation, not to model another tradition's problem in a solver class; 'tractable' means worst-case polynomial, the sense Method 1's Limitations date to 2004 [02 C2], though the same years also separate polynomial from practical (p. 22; S052 p. 4).

Claims 'the fastest way to solve them' from operation counts alone and concedes untested practicality: the practice SKILL.md's anti-pattern table rejects ('Polynomial solvability as the test of usefulness', remedied by measured solve times, Method 2).

Relaxation values are wanted as bounds for branch and bound and as the yardstick by which heuristics are judged (dual-ascent network design within 2–5% of optimality, judged against the LP relaxation): the certificate idea, without computation.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Computational success in IP is attributed to LP relaxations and Lagrangean duals, whose values feed branch and bound and judge heuristics; the paper speeds up their computation.

Dualize over an easy polyhedron so the dimension equals the number of complicating constraints and the subproblem optimizer becomes the separation oracle; cost splitting when separation is harder than optimization.

transferable: When a relaxation has few complicating constraints over an easy polyhedron, dualize over the polyhedron's extreme points: the dual's dimension is the number of complicating constraints and the subproblem optimizer is the separation oracle for any cutting-plane method (pp. 3–4).
If separation over a polyhedron is harder than optimization over it, split the variable (x1 = x2 = …) so each copy only needs optimization (p. 7; pp. 18–19).
Recover a primal optimum from the cut that is tight at the dual optimum instead of re-solving (Remark, p. 8).
Report algorithmic results as a problem / oracle / running-time table plus a comparison table against the best known method (Tables 1–3, pp. 11, 21).
State in the conclusion what a complexity result cannot show: untested practicality and dependence on a subroutine (p. 22).

quotes.text: In this paper we focus on problems already known to be solvable in polynomial time, but where ellipsoid like methods lead to significant computational speedups.
The practicality of our algorithm critically depends on whether Vaidya's algorithm is a practical algorithm, and to our knowledge Vaidya's algorithm has not been tested in practice.
